docs.title: 1. Homepage Identity
docs.text: This portfolio is a clear, organized record of my engineering work for MEGR 2157, built specifically for peer reviewers and hiring managers. Instead of acting as a personal resume, this site focuses on what the portfolio actually contains: structured technical assignments, analytical models, and documented design choices. The goal is to give readers a straightforward place to quickly locate, review, and verify my mechanical engineering calculations and decisions.

docs.title: 2. One Intentional Customization
docs.text:
• Changed Element: Added explicit structural section headers (1. Homepage Identity, 2. One Intentional Customization, 3. Your Documentation Standard) to the Part 2 submission block.
  • Functional Requirement: Improves information retrieval and visual hierarchy, allowing readers and evaluators to navigate to specific decision criteria in under 10 seconds.
  • Why Default Failed: The default unformatted body text created dense text blocks that reduced readability and slowed down systematic review.

docs.title: 3. Your Documentation Standard
docs.text: I commit to creating a clear and concise documentation that presents complete mathematical models, engineering assumptions, and justifications for every design decision. ## Part 1, Task A: Portfolio Analysis

docs.title: Professional Introduction
docs.text: My name is Caleb Burnham and I am an undergraduate mechanical engineering student studying at UNC Charlotte. My path to mechanical engineering grew from my desire to discover how objects operate in real world conditions. As an aspiring engineer I focus on approaching problems systematically by breaking them down into basic groups. Through my coursework and projects I am building skills in testing, documentation, and practical decision making. My goal is to build a strong engineering foundation that allows me to analyze designs critically, defend decisions and share clear work with engineering teams.

docs.title: Defending Engineering Decisions
docs.text: Defending an engineering decision means to mathematically and systematically defend any design decisions without any personal biases. You must demonstrate why your design is better than alternatives. Currently I understand the framework of defending a decision, such as identifying trade-offs and grounding choices in mechanical principles, but I am still developing the practical experience required to execute and validate complex engineering defenses under real-world constraints.

docs.title: Part 1, Task B: Product Analysis — Medium Binder Clip
a. Primary Engineering Function
docs.text: The primary engineering function of a binder clip is to apply a constant clamping force across a stack of material using spring tension to keep the sheets from sliding.

docs.title: b. Governing Model & Assumptions
docs.text: Key Assumption: The spring steel remains in its linear elastic range, meaning opening the clip never bends the metal permanently.

docs.title: c. Component Geometry & Mechanical Function
docs.text:
• Component 1: Sheet Steel Spring Body

  • Functionality: Formed into a triangular shape with folded edges. The rear curved spine acts as a hinge spring, while the flat sides transfer the spring force directly to the front gripping edges.

  • Components 2 & 3: Wire Handles (Pair)

  • Functionality: Bent wire loops that snap into the folded edges of the body. They act as levers to squeeze the clip open. Once attached, they pivot flat against the paper stack to save space.

docs.title: d. Patent Research
docs.text:
• Patent Number: US1139627A
  • Author(s): Louis E. Baltzley

docs.title: i. Alternative Solutions
docs.text:
1. Brass Paper Fastener: Uses bendable metal legs that fold manually rather than spring tension.
  2. Standard Wire Paperclip: Relies on torsional and bending of a single wire loop to pinch paper, providing a lighter clamping force without handles or multiple parts.

docs.title: ii. Key Engineering Design Decision
docs.text:
• Decision: Rolling the top and bottom edges of the steel body into round sockets.
  • Justification: This design creates a hinge socket to hold the wire handles while stiffening the metal edge so it does not bend out of shape under heavy clamping force.

docs.title: Assignment Effort
docs.text: Time spent on assignment: 3.5 hours

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Design a lightweight planar truss and connecting pins using standard material properties to safely support a specified load. I selected applied force magnitudes of 30 kN (+30 kN at Point C and -30 kN at Point D), with Point A configured as a pin support (Ay = +10 kN) and Point B as a roller support (By = -10 kN).

docs.title: 1. External Reactions & Internal Static Analysis
docs.text:
I started by creating quick hand sketches of potential truss geometries to connect all required nodes while minimizing structural weight. I selected a triangulated 5-member configuration (AB, AC, AD, BC, CD) because triangular units efficiently distribute large applied forces. I am aware that adding an extra pin in between A and B and creating 3 triangles would have created a more even distribution. However, application of the truss was not given and I wanted to create a simple truss that would be less time consuming to solve for.

Next, I solved for the external reaction forces by taking a moment equilibrium equation about Pin A, yielding vertical reaction forces of Ay = +10 kN at Pin A and By = -10 kN at Roller B. With the support reactions established, I determined internal member forces using the Method of Joints:

  • Joint B: Summed forces in the vertical direction to set the roller reaction equal to the vertical component of Member BC, yielding the force magnitude for BC. Summing forces horizontally gave the tension force in Member AB.
  • Joint C & Joint D: Calculated the member angles using trigonometry to resolve force components. I summed forces vertically and horizontally across Joints C and D, accounting for the applied loads of +30 kN at Joint C and -30 kN at Joint D.
  • Maximum Force: Comparing all internal member results revealed that Member AB experiences the largest internal force of 87.58 kN in compression.

docs.title: 2. Member Cross-Sectional Area & Frame Weight
docs.text:
Using the maximum compressive load, I calculated the required uniform cross-sectional area for all members:

  • Applied a safety factor of 3.5 against the yield strength of A500 structural steel.
  • Symbolically solved for minimum cross-sectional area: A_min = (F_max × FS) / σ_y
  • Numerically evaluated the required area: A_min = (87,580 N × 3.5) / σ_y

To determine total frame weight, I summed the total member lengths across members (AB, AC, AD, BC, CD), multiplied by A_min to find the total steel volume, and applied the density of steel:

Weight_frame = Volume × density × g

docs.title: 3. Single-Shear Pin Sizing & Pin Weight
docs.text:
Next, I sized the connecting pins located at joints A, B, C, and D:

  • Material & Safety Factor: Hardened tool steel with a yield shear strength τ_y = 170 ksi (1.1721 × 10⁹ N/m²), density ρ_pin = 7694 kg/m³, and a safety factor of 4.0 under single shear (n = 1).
  • Symbolic Pin Area: τ_allow = τ_y / FS = V_max / A_pin → A_pin = (V_max × FS) / τ_y
  • Numerical Pin Area: A_pin = (87,580 N × 4.0) / (1.1721 × 10⁹ N/m²) = 298.9 mm² (Radius r = 9.755 mm, Diameter d = 19.51 mm)

For a square member profile (31.1 mm × 31.1 mm cross-section giving area 967 mm²), the pin length spanning a single-shear joint between two overlapping members is L_pin = 2 × 31.1 mm = 62.2 mm (0.0622 m). Calculating the combined volume for all 4 pins gave a total pin weight of:

Weight_pins = 4 × A_pin × L_pin × ρ_pin × g = 5.61 N (0.572 kg)

docs.title: 4. CAD Modeling & Weight Verification
docs.text:
After completing hand calculations, I modeled the 3D geometry in CAD:

  • Extruded the truss frame as a single part, maintaining a constant member cross-section of 967 mm² (31.1 mm × 31.1 mm square profile).
  • Modeled the 4 joint pins as cylindrical parts with a diameter of 19.51 mm (A_pin = 298.9 mm²) and length of 62.2 mm.
  • Assigned material mass densities to both parts in CAD and evaluated software Mass Properties.

Click here to download assembly

The CAD model mass properties closely matched the hand calculations (257.2 N for the truss frame and 5.61 N for the pins). Small variances are due to joint node overlaps where member ends meet at pin locations.

docs.title: Decide
docs.text: I selected a 5-member planar triangulated geometry because it minimizes total member count and overall structural weight while maintaining high rigidity under vertical loads. Choosing a square profile (31.1 mm × 31.1 mm) provided a uniform extrusion thickness that cleanly accommodated single-shear pin connections at each joint node.

docs.title: Engineering Lessons Learned
docs.text:
• Yield Strength vs. External Stress Sizing: I learned how to size structural elements by directly comparing allowable internal stress against material yield strength modified by safety factors, ensuring structural integrity without adding unnecessary material weight.
  • Joint Thickness & Pin Weight Interaction: I discovered that pin length depends directly on beam cross-sectional geometry in single-shear joints, meaning thicker member profiles increase total pin engagement length and directly add hardware weight.
  • Hand Calculation vs. CAD Verification: I realized the importance of computing physical mass properties by hand prior to modeling in CAD, allowing me to verify material density assignments and catch dimensional errors during software evaluation. This assignment took roughly 5 hours of work. Longest part was getting the portfolio set up.
